## Overview and grading

### What you'll practice

In this graded assignment, you will first write a shell script to run the
program TrimGalore, run it, and interpret its output, all **without** genAI.
Then, you will hand your script to Claude Code:
you'll have it review and extend your script, write a loop to run the script
for multiple samples, and summarize the results.
Along the way, you'll critically check what Claude produces,
and document your genAI use.

### Submission expectations

- **Deadline**: [Sunday Oct 25^th^ at 11:59 pm]{style="background-color: #faf678;"}.
- **Submission**: Like for GA3, you will submit your assignment by tagging the
  instructors in an Issue in your GitHub repository, as per the last step below.

::: callout-note
#### Oral examination
As explained in [GA3](GA3.qmd#oral-exam),
each of you will have **one** short oral examination,
for one of GA3, GA4, or GA5.
If you already had yours for GA3, you won't have another one.
If not, it may be for this assignment,
in which case you should also be able to explain any code that genAI wrote for you.
:::

### GenAI expectations

This is the first assignment in which you are allowed to use generative AI.
Now that we've covered these tools in weeks 8 and 9,
the course guideline from here on (including for the Final Project) applies:

- You may use genAI, **as long as you can explain what your code does**.
  If genAI produces commands or constructs that we have not covered in class,
  do the research needed to understand them.
- Whatever the source, **you remain responsible for whether the code is correct**.
  "The AI told me so" is not a defense for a wrong answer.

That said, this assignment has two exceptions:

- You must do **Part B without** genAI assistance.
  This is because in Part C, you'll compare genAI output with
  a script and answers you produced yourself.
  As in GA3, for any use of commands or options in Part B that we didn't cover
  in the course, provide the specific source.
- In Part C, on the other hand, you are _required_ to use Claude Code and to
  document how you used it.
:::

### Rubric

You can earn a maximum of **0.5 points** for each of the 20 numbered questions/items below.
There are two **bonus** questions (21 and 22) that can also earn you 0.5 points
each, but only in case you dropped points elsewhere.

### Part B: A TrimGalore script --- without genAI

TrimGalore [@krueger2021] is a commonly used tool to preprocess the reads
in FASTQ files before further analysis.
It's the next step in the RNA-seq analysis workflow we're gradually applying to
the @garrigós2025 data in this course:

![](/img/rnaseq-wf-3.png){fig-align="center" width="60%" fig-alt="A diagram showing the steps in an RNA-seq analysis pipeline." .lightbox}

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

TrimGalore takes FASTQ files as input, and removes:

- Any adapter sequences that are present in the reads^[
  Adapters are always added to DNA/cDNA fragments of interest prior to Illumina sequencing,
  and the last bases of a read can "read-through" into the adapter if the fragment
  is shorter than the read length.]
- Poor-quality bases at the end of the reads
- Reads that have become very short after the prior two steps

It then writes the filtered reads to new FASTQ files.
But unlike FastQC, you don't run it on one FASTQ file at a time.
When you have paired-end reads, like with the @garrigós2025 data,
a **single** TrimGalore run should include **both** the R1 (forward read) and
R2 (reverse read) file for one sample.
This is because R1 and R2 files need to remain "synced":
generally, you can't remove a read from an R1 file without also removing
its mate from the R2 file.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### More about TrimGalore and similar programs _(Click to expand)_

Several largely equivalent tools exist for this kind of FASTQ preprocessing ---
[Trimmomatic](http://www.usadellab.org/cms/index.php?page=trimmomatic) and
[fastp](https://github.com/OpenGene/fastp) are two other commonly used ones.
TrimGalore itself is "just" a wrapper around yet another tool called Cutadapt,
but it is simpler to use.
Two advantages of TrimGalore are:

- It will auto-detect the adapters that are present in your reads.
- It can automatically run FastQC on the trimmed sequences.
:::

03. Get a link from the Seqera Containers website to a **container** with
    TrimGalore version 2.3.0.

04. Print TrimGalore's help info by running `trim_galore --help` with your
    container link. Use the help info to find the options to:
    - Tell TrimGalore that the reads in your input FASTQ files are **paired-end**^[
      If you don't do this, TrimGalore will process the two FASTQ files independently.]
    - Set the **output dir**
    - Make it **run FastQC** on the trimmed FASTQ files

05. Also use the help info to find the **default thresholds** for the
    base quality score and the read length.
    In your own words, what does TrimGalore do with each of these thresholds?
    For example, will it remove a low-quality base in the middle of a read?
    _(You don't have to change these thresholds, the defaults work fine for us.)_

06. Write a shell script `scripts/trimgalore.sh` that runs TrimGalore
    on the R1 and R2 FASTQ files of **one** sample:
    - The script should accept three arguments:
      the R1 FASTQ file, the R2 FASTQ file, and the output dir.
    - Use the three options from question 4.
    - Include "logging statements" with `echo`, like in the FastQC script from class,
      and a line that prints the TrimGalore version.

    <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} Click here for a hint</summary>
    Use your `fastqc.sh` script from [class](/week07/w7b_scripts2.qmd#your-fastqc-script)
    as a starting point,
    and recall how you ran a script for a pair of FASTQ files in the
    [w7b self-study exercise](/week07/w7b_scripts2.qmd#self-study-looping-over-samples).
    </details>

    ::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
    #### Don't use TrimGalore's `--cores` option for now _(Click to expand)_
    Since you're running the program interactively on your single-core VS Code compute job,
    you only have 1 core at your disposal --- and that's TrimGalore's default.
    Therefore, don't adjust this setting here.
    Next week, you'll learn to submit scripts as batch jobs,
    which gives you the opportunity to use multiple cores.

07. Run your script for the FASTQ files of sample `S63`,
    with `results/trimgalore` as the output dir.
    Then, list the files in the output dir,
    and briefly describe what each _type_ of output file contains.
    Once your script works, commit it.
    _(If something went wrong, go back to your script and try to fix it,_
    _and briefly describe the problem and your fix in the README.)_

08. TrimGalore printed a lot of output to the screen,
    most of which is also saved in its `*_trimming_report.txt` output files.
    Use this output to answer the following:
    - In each file (R1 and R2), in what percentage of reads were adapters detected?
    - In each file (R1 and R2), what percentage of bases were quality-trimmed?
    - What percentage of read pairs were removed because they were too short?

09. Compare TrimGalore's FastQC report for the **trimmed** R1 file with
    the FastQC report for the **raw** R1 file of the same sample
    (for example, from your GA3 dir: `../GA3/results/fastqc/S63_R1_fastqc.html`).
    - Name at least two differences between the reports.
    - Do the short reads with only `N`s,
      which you saw [in week 4](/week04/w4c_shell-files2.qmd#less-to-page-through-files),
      appear to have been removed?
      The example read in week 4 was 35 bp long,
      which is longer than TrimGalore's default length threshold.
      So how could TrimGalore have removed it?

### Part C: Bring in genAI

Now that you have a script that you wrote yourself and that you know works,
you'll use Claude Code to review and extend it.

- Use the Claude extension in VS Code, as in [class](/week09/w9a_claude.qmd),
  and keep the permission mode at **Manual** throughout.
- Start a new conversation for each question,
  to keep the context window small (and to save costs).
- For each question, record in your README what you asked,
  what you got, and what you concluded after checking it.
- You are graded on your evaluation of Claude's output,
  not on whether Claude happened to give a good answer.
  A well-documented case in which you caught Claude being wrong
  is worth full points.

11. With your `scripts/trimgalore.sh` open in the editor, and the Claude panel open,
    check that the script is added as context
    (you should see its name below the prompt box).
    Then, ask Claude to **review** your script, for example:

    > Review this shell script. What could be wrong with it, and what would you improve?
    > Don't change the script yet.

    In your README, briefly list Claude's suggestions,
    and for each, say whether and why you agree with it, disagree with it,
    or don't understand it.
    Did it suggest anything that you think is wrong,
    or that conflicts with how we've been writing scripts in this course?
    Did it refer to any of the conventions in your `CLAUDE.md`?

12. Before making changes, run your script with a file path that doesn't exist.
    What happens, and at which point does the script stop?

13. Ask Claude to add a check to your script, for example:

    > Add a check that both input FASTQ files exist, and exit with an informative
    > error message if they don't

    Claude will show you the proposed change as a diff:
    read it before you accept it.
    Then, **test** the updated script with the same non-existent file name as above.
    Does it behave the way Claude claimed it would?
    And given what you saw in the previous question, how useful is this check?

    Finally, **commit** the updated script.
    Your Git history now shows exactly what Claude changed in your script.

14. Ask Claude to write a `for` loop that runs your script for multiple samples,
    for example:

    > Write a for loop that runs scripts/trimgalore.sh for the 7 samples whose IDs
    > start with S6, with output dir results/trimgalore.
    > I will run the loop from the GA4 dir.
    > Only show me the loop: don't add it to a file, and don't run it.

    Add the loop to your README,
    and **before** running it, compare this to what you learned in the
    [w7b self-study section](/week07/w7b_scripts2.qmd#self-study-looping-over-samples):

    - Does it run the script once per sample, rather than once per FASTQ file?
    - Does it get the correct R2 file for each R1 file?
      If you don't understand how it does this, ask Claude to explain that part.
      Would Claude's approach have the `S61` pitfall from the w7b self-study exercise?
    - Does it only include the 7 `S6` samples?

    If you had to fix the loop, explain what you changed and why.

15. Test the loop by putting `echo` before the `bash` command,
    so that it only prints the commands it would run.
    If those look right, remove the `echo` and run the loop for real
    (this will take about 10 minutes).
    When it's done, how many files do you expect to be in `results/trimgalore`,
    and is that what you find?

16. Ask Claude for a command that produces a small **summary table**
    of all your TrimGalore results,
    with one line per sample and the percentage of read pairs that were removed
    because they were too short.
    Run the command, and **verify** its output:
    - Does the value for `S63` match your answer to question 8?
    - In your own words, how does the command work?
      If it uses anything we didn't cover in class, ask Claude to explain it.

17. **Document** your genAI use by saving your Part C conversations
    with the `/export` command, as shown in
    [class](/week09/w9a_claude.qmd#documenting-ai-use).
    Save them in a dir `doc/ai` in your working dir, with descriptive file names,
    and commit them to your Git repo.

18. Write a short **reflection** in your README (one or two paragraphs):
    in [class](/week09/w9a_claude.qmd), Claude wrote a script from scratch,
    while here, you wrote the script yourself first.
    Which approach gave you more confidence that the script is correct, and why?
    Also, did Claude tell you anything during this assignment that turned out to
    be wrong, and how did you find out?

21. Ask Claude for help with something related to this assignment that you
    genuinely don't know how to do yourself.
    Some ideas:
    - Comparing the file sizes of the FASTQ files before and after trimming,
      in a small summary table
    - Counting the number of reads in each trimmed FASTQ file
    - Anything else you're curious about

    Run the code you get, and describe how you checked that it does what you
    think it does.
    Also export this conversation to `doc/ai`.

22. Based on your experiences in this part,
    add one or more instructions to your `CLAUDE.md` that would have improved
    Claude's output
    (for example, to prevent a suggestion you disagreed with in question 11).
    Then, start a new conversation and test whether Claude follows the new instruction.
    In your README, describe what you added and what happened,
    and commit your updated `CLAUDE.md`.
